newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ogata hopeful HK to maintain humane asylum policy.
newsitem.headline: Ogata hopeful HK to maintain humane asylum policy.

text.p: The head of the United Nations refugee agency said on Monday she was hopeful Hong Kong would maintain a humane asylum policy after the British territory returned to Chinese sovereignty this year.

U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata said she told Tung Chee-hwa, who will be the territory's first chief executive after the handover, at a meeting on Monday that the world needed Hong Kong to continue providing a humanitarian refuge.
"I did make this point and my impression is that he will continue this humane tradition," Ogata told a news conference.
"He himself came from Shanghai, he said," she added. Tung's family fled to Hong Kong from the Chinese city before the communist take over of China in 1949.
But Ogata did not specify what might happen to Vietnamese boat people remaining in Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
More than 5,000 boat people are still in Hong Kong camps, the last of more than 200,000 that landed here after fleeing their homeland following the communist victory in southern Vietnam in 1975.
China has demanded that the camps be cleared before the change in sovereignty, but Hong Kong authorities have admitted that this is unlikely.
About 1,300 Vietnamese are categorised as genuine refugees eligible for resettlement in third countries, but many have histories of crime or drug use that have made resettlement difficult.

Nearly 4,000 are regarded as economic migrants who must return home, but they must be recognised by Hanoi as its nationals, putting in question the status of many in the camps, including ethnic Chinese.
Ogata said she was optimistic that about 2,000 of the non-refugees would be cleared by Hanoi before Hong Kong's handover, and increasing that number would be her challenge.

"For the 1,300 refugees...I will be appealing to the resettlement countries once more, very strongly, giving certain cases of people who may have some record that is not the most desirable but I think on humanitarian grounds should be re-examined," she said.

Ogata held out little hope that Hong Kong would get back the more than HK$1 billion (US$130 million) it has paid on behalf of the United Nations for the upkeep of refugee camps and detention centres. "I do not have any money," she said. "Right now, I am trying desperately to raise money for the refugees in the great lakes region of Africa."
But Ogata said she would raise Hong Kong's case with donor nations.

Before the news conference, Ogata was met by a group of protesters demanding that the United Nations immediately repay Hong Kong's costs for keeping the refugees, and that the world body should take any refugees left in the territory before the handover. ($1 = HK$7.74)
